docs.title: PinGoblin Dual DC Motor Board
docs.text:
Board A drives two brushed DC motors in both directions (or four in one direction) from a Raspberry Pi, ESP32, Raspberry Pi Pico or any other 3.3 V or 5 V microcontroller. It uses two TI DRV8874 H-bridges, runs from a 6–18 V motor supply, and adds current sensing, protection and test buttons.

This site is the reference for the board and its software. It has two parts:

  • User Guide

    Setting up and using the board: specifications, safety, wiring, the J3 pinout, current sensing, the PMODE jumper and troubleshooting.

  • API

    The pingoblin_motor library for the Raspberry Pi, and the single-file version for MicroPython (ESP32 and Pico): stall and fault detection, current sensing and daisy-chained boards.

docs.title: Ten-second example
docs.text:
Raspberry PiMicroPython (ESP32) 
from pingoblin_motor import MotorBoard

board = MotorBoard(a_en=12, a_ph=5, b_en=13, b_ph=6, sleep_pin=26, fault_pin=19)
board.start_monitor()                              # stall and fault detection
board.motor_a.forward(60, duration=2, wait=True)   # 60 % for 2 s, then brake
board.close()

from pingoblin_motor import MotorBoard

board = MotorBoard(a_en=25, a_ph=26, b_en=27, b_ph=33, sleep_pin=32, fault_pin=39)
board.enable_monitor(on_fault=print)
board.motor_a.forward(60, duration=2, wait=True)

The source, hardware notes and issue tracker are on GitHub. Everything is released under the MIT licence.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
pingoblin_motor controls PinGoblin Board A from Python. There are two versions with the same classes and method names, so code moves between them with little change:

Version Runs on Install Raspberry Pi package (python/) Raspberry Pi with Python 3.8+ and gpiozero (Pi 5 supported) pip install ".[pi]" MicroPython module (micropython/) ESP32, Raspberry Pi Pico / Pico 2, MicroPython 1.20+ mpremote mip install github:PinGoblin/DRV8874/micropython

Both handle one board or many daisy-chained boards, optional current sensing, and fault detection that includes stalled motors.

from pingoblin_motor import MotorBoard

board = MotorBoard(a_en=12, a_ph=5, b_en=13, b_ph=6, sleep_pin=26, fault_pin=19)
board.start_monitor()                              # Pi; on MicroPython: enable_monitor()

board.motor_a.forward(60, duration=2, wait=True)   # 60 % for 2 s, then brake
board.motor_b.reverse(40)
board.motor_b.speed_pc = 80                        # change speed while running
board.motor_b.coast()                              # spin down freely
board.close()

docs.text: The Raspberry Pi reference documents each module of the package. The main classes are MotorBoard, Motor and MotorChain; all are importable from pingoblin_motor. The MicroPython reference documents the single-file module.

docs.title: Creating a board
docs.text:
from pingoblin_motor import MotorBoard

board = MotorBoard(
    "front",                     # board name, used in "front.a"
    a_en=12, a_ph=5,             # J3 pins 3, 4
    b_en=13, b_ph=6,             # J3 pins 5, 6 (optional)
    sleep_pin=26,                # J3 pin 9 (optional; needed for coast in PH/EN mode)
    fault_pin=19,                # J3 pin 10 (optional; needed for stall detection without a sensor)
    mode="ph_en",                # "ph_en" (JP1 pads 1-2, default), "pwm" (JP1 pads 2-3)
                                 # or "independent" (JP1 open: four-motor mode)
    logic_voltage=3.3,           # VLOGIC: sets the current limit (about 2.0 A at 3.3 V, 3.0 A at 5 V)
    motor_names=("left", "right"),
    motor_options=dict(ramp_time=0.5),   # options for both motors
)

Boards work as context managers (with MotorBoard(...) as board:), which brake the motors and release the pins on exit.

docs.title: Speed and direction
docs.text:
Speed is a percentage, 0–100. Direction is chosen by the method:

m = board.motor_a
m.forward(60)              # 60 % forward
m.reverse(40)              # 40 % reverse
m.run(-25)                 # signed: negative = reverse, 0 = stop
m.speed_pc = 80            # change speed while running
m.start()                  # resume the last direction and speed
m.forward(50, duration=2)  # stop after 2 s (returns at once)
m.forward(50, duration=2, wait=True)   # ... and block until it stops

Useful motor options (pass in motor_options=, a_options= or b_options=):

Option Default Meaning invert False Swap forward and reverse (instead of swapping wires) min_speed_pc 0 Raise any non-zero speed to at least this (motor deadband) ramp_time 0 Seconds to ramp 0→100 %. Soft start and soft speed changes reverse_delay 0.1 Brake time before reversing a running motor

The fault-detection options are covered in Faults. The full list is in the Motor reference.

docs.title: Stop, brake and coast
docs.text:
Call Outputs Effect stop() / brake() Both low Motor stops quickly coast() Open Motor spins down freely board.sleep() Open, both motors Both drivers sleep (near-zero current)

In PH/EN mode the DRV8874 can only coast by sleeping, and nSLEEP is shared by both motors on a board (and by every board wired to the same GPIO). coast() therefore sleeps the line only if every other motor on it is idle. Otherwise it brakes and returns False. In PWM mode (mode="pwm"), each motor coasts independently.

docs.title: Four-motor mode
docs.text:
With JP1 open, mode="independent" gives four HalfBridgeMotors instead of two motors. Each runs one way only and is driven by one input pin: A_EN → a1, A_PH → a2, B_EN → b1, B_PH → b2.

board = MotorBoard(a_en=12, a_ph=5, b_en=13, b_ph=6, sleep_pin=26, fault_pin=19,
                   mode="independent", motor_names=("pump", "fan", "valve", "light"))
board["pump"].forward(60)           # 60 % (the library inverts the pin duty for you)
board["valve"].forward(100, duration=0.5)
board.driver_current("a")           # pump + fan together, if a sensor is configured
  • sleep_pin is required. The drivers stay asleep until the first run command, and close() puts them to sleep before releasing the pins. Fit the 4.7 kΩ nSLEEP pull-down described in Four-motor mode, so the motors stay off whenever your program isn't running.
  • reverse(), negative speeds and invert raise errors. board.motor_a and board.motor_b raise ConfigError: use the names.
  • coast() sleeps the drivers, so it only coasts when every other motor on the nSLEEP line is idle.
  • The fault monitor reports DRIVER_FAULT (nFAULT low) and, with sensors, BOARD_OVERLOAD. There are no per-motor stall, open-load or overload checks.

docs.title: PWM frequency
docs.text:
On the Raspberry Pi, gpiozero uses software PWM. The default of 1 kHz works on any GPIO but makes motors whine. For silent 20 kHz, use the hardware PWM pins (GPIO12, 13, 18 or 19) for the EN lines:

from pingoblin_motor import GpiozeroBackend, MotorBoard

backend = GpiozeroBackend(hardware_pwm=True, pwm_chip=0)   # pwm_chip=2 on some Pi 5 kernels
board = MotorBoard(a_en=12, a_ph=5, b_en=13, b_ph=6, backend=backend, pwm_frequency=20000)

This needs dtoverlay=pwm-2chan in /boot/firmware/config.txt and the rpi-hardware-pwm package. The Pi has two hardware PWM channels, so it covers two motors (one board).

MicroPython boards use hardware PWM on any pin at 20 kHz by default (pwm_freq=).

docs.title: Thread safety (Raspberry Pi)
docs.text: Motor commands are protected by a lock, so you can call them from several threads. The fault monitor, duration timers and ramps run in daemon threads. Fault handlers run on the monitor thread, so keep them short.

docs.title: Current sensing
docs.text: Board A's ISENSE outputs give 0.675 V per amp (see the User Guide). The library turns that into amps on motor.current, and uses it for stall, overload and open-load detection.

docs.title: PinGoblin ADS1115 board
docs.text:
The Raspberry Pi has no ADC, so use a PinGoblin ADS1115 board. Wire A_ISENSE and B_ISENSE (J3 pins 7, 8) to the ADS1115 inputs. One ADS1115 reads two boards, and up to four ADS1115 boards share the I2C bus (addresses 0x48–0x4B).

Raspberry PiMicroPython 
from pingoblin_motor import ADS1115, MotorBoard

adc = ADS1115(bus=1, address=0x48)
board = MotorBoard(a_en=12, a_ph=5, b_en=13, b_ph=6, fault_pin=19,
                   adc=adc, a_sense_channel=0, b_sense_channel=1)
board.motor_a.forward(70)
print(f"{board.motor_a.current:.2f} A")

from machine import I2C, Pin
from pingoblin_motor import ADS1115, MotorBoard

i2c = I2C(0, sda=Pin(21), scl=Pin(22), freq=400000)   # Pico: I2C(0, sda=Pin(0), scl=Pin(1))
adc = ADS1115(i2c, address=0x48)
board = MotorBoard(a_en=25, a_ph=26, b_en=27, b_ph=33, fault_pin=39,
                   adc=adc, a_sense_channel=0, b_sense_channel=1)

ISENSE is zero during the PWM off-time. The ADS1115 averages each reading over about 1.2 ms, so the library divides by the PWM duty to estimate the motor current. Below 10 % duty the estimate is unreliable, so the raw reading is returned.

docs.title: The microcontroller's own ADC (MicroPython)
docs.text:
from pingoblin_motor import ADCChannel, MotorBoard

board = MotorBoard(a_en=25, a_ph=26, b_en=27, b_ph=33, fault_pin=39,
                   a_sensor=ADCChannel(34), b_sensor=ADCChannel(35))

The built-in ADC takes instant samples, so with PWM each one is either the full motor current or zero. The library averages 16 samples per reading, which gives a usable mean but is noisier than the ADS1115. On the Pico, ISENSE is read against the 3.3 V supply (ADCChannel(26, vref=3.3)).

docs.title: Board and chain totals
docs.text:
board.total_current and chain.total_current add up the motor currents. They drive the BOARD_OVERLOAD (3 A fuse) and CHAIN_OVERLOAD (6 A terminals) checks.

Note

ISENSE measures load, not speed. A free-running motor draws about the same current at any speed.

docs.title: Daisy-chained boards
docs.text:
Each board has its own EN/PH pins. nSLEEP and nFAULT can be shared: wire them together and pass the same GPIO to every board, which gives one e-stop line and one fault line. See Daisy-chaining boards for the wiring and current limits.

from pingoblin_motor import ADS1115, MotorBoard, MotorChain

adc = ADS1115(address=0x48)
front = MotorBoard("front", a_en=12, a_ph=5, b_en=13, b_ph=6, sleep_pin=26, fault_pin=19,
                   adc=adc, a_sense_channel=0, b_sense_channel=1)
rear = MotorBoard("rear", a_en=16, a_ph=20, b_en=21, b_ph=7, sleep_pin=26, fault_pin=19,
                  adc=adc, a_sense_channel=2, b_sense_channel=3)

with MotorChain([front, rear]) as chain:          # starts the fault monitor
    chain.alias("left", "front.a")
    chain.alias("right", "front.b")
    chain["left"].forward(50)
    chain["rear.a"].reverse(30, duration=1.5)
    chain.add_fault_handler(print)
    ...
    chain.emergency_stop()                        # brake all, then sleep all boards

Motors are addressed as "board.motor" (for example "front.a"), or by an alias. MotorChain also has stop_all(), coast_all(), faults (history), active_faults, clear_faults(), total_current and check_faults().

docs.title: Faults and stall detection
docs.text:
Start the fault monitor with board.start_monitor() (Raspberry Pi), board.enable_monitor() (MicroPython), or by creating a MotorChain.

FaultType Detected when Needs a current sensor? Default action Latches STALL Current ≥ stall_current for stall_time while driven, or nFAULT low (current limiting) for stall_time without a sensor No Brake Yes CURRENT_LIMIT nFAULT low while driven (warning, at most every 5 s) No None No DRIVER_FAULT nFAULT low for 0.2 s with no motor driven: output short, overcurrent or over-temperature shutdown No Sleep board (brake if no sleep pin) Yes OPEN_LOAD Under 30 mA for 1 s while driven at ≥ 20 %: motor disconnected, broken wire, motor supply off or fuse tripped Yes Brake Yes OVERLOAD Over continuous_current for overload_time Yes Brake Yes BOARD_OVERLOAD Board supply current over the 3 A fuse rating for 1 s Yes Brake No CHAIN_OVERLOAD Daisy-chain supply current over 6 A for 1 s Yes Brake No SENSOR_ERROR Current-sensor read fails (reported once until it recovers) Yes None No

Without a sensor, a stall is inferred from nFAULT. If both motors on a board are running, the board can't tell which one stalled, so both are stopped.

docs.title: Reacting to faults
docs.text:
from pingoblin_motor import FaultAction, FaultPolicy, FaultType, MotorBoard

def on_fault(fault):
    print(fault)              # [stall] front.a: motor stalled: 1.82 A for 0.5 s

# Per-motor policy: coast on stall, and don't latch
policy = FaultPolicy({FaultType.STALL: FaultAction.COAST}, latch=False)
board = MotorBoard(a_en=12, a_ph=5, fault_pin=19, a_options=dict(policy=policy))
board.start_monitor(on_fault=on_fault)

board.motor_a.add_fault_handler(lambda f: print("motor A:", f.message))

A latched fault stops the motor and blocks it: commanding it raises MotorFaultError until you clear it.

board.motor_a.clear_fault()

docs.title: Stall homing
docs.text:
Driving into an end stop and stopping on the stall is a cheap way to home an axis:

from pingoblin_motor import FaultAction, FaultPolicy, FaultType, MotorBoard

policy = FaultPolicy({FaultType.STALL: FaultAction.BRAKE}, latch=False)
board = MotorBoard(a_en=12, a_ph=5, fault_pin=19,
                   a_options=dict(policy=policy, stall_time=0.2))
board.start_monitor()
board.motor_a.reverse(40)
board.motor_a.wait(timeout=10)       # returns when the stall brakes the motor

See python/examples/stall_homing.py and micropython/examples/pico_asyncio_stall_homing.py.

docs.title: Four-motor mode
docs.text: With mode="independent" the drivers don't limit current, so nFAULT low always means a driver shutdown and is reported as DRIVER_FAULT, even while motors run. STALL, CURRENT_LIMIT, OPEN_LOAD and OVERLOAD aren't detected, because ISENSE carries two motors at once. With a sensor on each driver, BOARD_OVERLOAD and CHAIN_OVERLOAD still work. See Four-motor mode.

docs.title: Raspberry Pi
docs.text:
The package needs Python 3.8+ and gpiozero. It is not on PyPI yet, so install it from the repository:

git clone https://github.com/PinGoblin/DRV8874.git
cd DRV8874/python
pip install ".[pi]"              # gpiozero and smbus2
pip install rpi-hardware-pwm     # optional: silent 20 kHz hardware PWM

smbus2 is only needed for current sensing through a PinGoblin ADS1115 board. Enable I2C with sudo raspi-config (Interface Options → I2C) if you use one.

Pin numbers are BCM GPIO numbers.

docs.title: MicroPython (ESP32, Pico)
docs.text:
Needs MicroPython 1.20 or later.

From GitHub with mip (on a Wi-Fi board, or through mpremote):

mpremote mip install github:PinGoblin/DRV8874/micropython

Or copy the file:

mpremote cp micropython/pingoblin_motor.py :

Precompile on ESP32

The source is about 63 KB, much of it docstrings, and compiling it on the board can run out of RAM on an ESP32 without PSRAM. Precompile it and copy the .mpy instead. .mpy files leave the docstrings out.

pip install mpy-cross
mpy-cross micropython/pingoblin_motor.py      # makes pingoblin_motor.mpy
mpremote cp micropython/pingoblin_motor.mpy :

Use an mpy-cross version that matches the board's MicroPython version.

docs.title: MicroPython notes
docs.text:
The MicroPython version is one file, micropython/pingoblin_motor.py, for ESP32 and Raspberry Pi Pico / Pico 2. It has the same classes and method names as the Raspberry Pi package.

Status

Tested off-target (CPython with mock pins, plus a static check for MicroPython-only syntax and modules, and CI runs under the MicroPython Unix port). It has not yet been run on a real ESP32 or Pico. Please report problems as GitHub issues.

docs.title: How timing works (no threads)
docs.text:
MicroPython has no threading.Timer, so timed runs (duration=), ramps (ramp_time) and fault checks all happen inside update(). Run it in one of three ways:

Style How asyncio (recommended) asyncio.create_task(board.run_monitor()). It calls update() every 20 ms Blocking helpers motor.forward(..., duration=2, wait=True), motor.wait(), board.pause(seconds). These call update() while they wait Your own loop Call board.update() every 10–50 ms

If nothing calls update(), a duration= run won't stop on its own, a ramp won't progress, and no faults are detected.

import asyncio
from pingoblin_motor import MotorBoard

board = MotorBoard(a_en=2, a_ph=3, b_en=4, b_ph=5, sleep_pin=6, fault_pin=7)
board.enable_monitor(on_fault=print)

async def main():
    asyncio.create_task(board.run_monitor())
    board.motor_a.forward(70, duration=3)
    while board.motor_a.busy:
        await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
    board.motor_a.reverse(40)
    await asyncio.sleep(2)
    board.stop_all()

asyncio.run(main())

The full API is in the MicroPython reference.

docs.title: Testing without hardware
docs.text:
Both versions include mock pins and a mock current sensor, so you can develop and test on any computer.

Raspberry Pi packageMicroPython module 
from pingoblin_motor import MockBackend, MockCurrentSensor, MotorBoard

sensor = MockCurrentSensor()
board = MotorBoard(a_en=12, a_ph=5, backend=MockBackend(), a_sensor=sensor)
board.motor_a.forward(50)
sensor.amps = 1.9          # simulate a stall

from pingoblin_motor import MockPins, MockSensor, MotorBoard

board = MotorBoard(a_en=1, a_ph=2, pins=MockPins(), a_sensor=MockSensor())

The MicroPython file also runs under CPython, which is how its tests run.

docs.title: Running the test suites
docs.text:
cd python && python -m pytest                 # Raspberry Pi package
cd micropython && python -m pytest tests      # MicroPython module, under CPython

CI also runs a smoke test under the MicroPython Unix port, checks that the file precompiles with mpy-cross, and builds this documentation with mkdocs build --strict.

docs.title: Pin backends
docs.text:
Hardware pin backends.

A backend creates three kinds of pin: digital outputs, PWM outputs and digital inputs. Pins are cached by GPIO number, so several boards in a daisy chain can share one nSLEEP or nFAULT line: ask for the same pin twice and you get the same object back. A shared pin is released when the last user closes it.

Backend Use GpiozeroBackend Default on a Raspberry Pi (Pi 5 supported). Software PWM, or hardware PWM on GPIO12/13/18/19 MockBackend No hardware: tests, dry runs and CI

MotorBoard(name: str = 'board', *, a_en: int, a_ph: int, b_en: Optional[int] = None, b_ph: Optional[int] = None, sleep_pin: Optional[int] = None, fault_pin: Optional[int] = None, mode: str = 'ph_en', logic_voltage: float = 3.3, adc: Optional[ADS1115] = None, a_sense_channel: Optional[int] = None, b_sense_channel: Optional[int] = None, sense_samples: int = 4, a_sensor: Optional[CurrentSensor] = None, b_sensor: Optional[CurrentSensor] = None, backend: Optional[Backend] = None, pwm_frequency: float = 1000.0, motor_names=None, motor_options: Optional[dict] = None, a_options: Optional[dict] = None, b_options: Optional[dict] = None, fuse_rating: float = 3.0)

One Board A dual DC motor driver.

Pins are BCM GPIO numbers. Motor B is optional. Several boards can share sleep_pin (one e-stop line) and fault_pin (wired-OR fault line): pass the same GPIO to each board. Boards work as context managers and close on exit.

The mode must match the PMODE jumper JP1:

mode JP1 Motors Names (default) "ph_en" Pads 1–2 (default) 2 × Motor a, b "pwm" Pads 2–3 2 × Motor a, b "independent" All pads open 4 × HalfBridgeMotor a1, a2, b1, b2 Example 
from pingoblin_motor import MotorBoard

with MotorBoard(a_en=12, a_ph=5, b_en=13, b_ph=6,
                sleep_pin=26, fault_pin=19) as board:
    board.start_monitor(on_fault=print)
    board.motor_a.forward(60, duration=2, wait=True)
Four-motor mode 
with MotorBoard(a_en=12, a_ph=5, b_en=13, b_ph=6, sleep_pin=26, fault_pin=19,
                mode="independent") as board:
    board["a1"].forward(50)
    board["b2"].forward(80, duration=2, wait=True)

In this mode an input that isn't driven turns its motor on. The board must have sleep_pin wired, with a 4.7 kΩ resistor from J3 pin 9 to GND, so the drivers sleep whenever your program isn't holding nSLEEP high. The library keeps the drivers asleep until the first run command, and puts them to sleep in close().

docs.title: MicroPython reference
docs.text:
The MicroPython module is imported as pingoblin_motor on the board. It is documented here as pingoblin_motor_mp so it doesn't clash with the Raspberry Pi package.

pingoblin_motor for MicroPython: the PinGoblin Board A (2 × DRV8874) motor library in one file.

Runs on ESP32 and Raspberry Pi Pico / Pico 2 with MicroPython 1.20 or later, and has the same class and method names as the Raspberry Pi library: MotorBoard, Motor, HalfBridgeMotor (four-motor mode), MotorChain, forward(), reverse(), run(), start(), stop() / brake(), coast(), speed_pc and current.

There are no threads. Timed runs, ramps and fault checks happen in update(), which must be called in one of three ways:

  • as an asyncio task: asyncio.create_task(board.run_monitor());
  • through the blocking helpers: board.pause(2) or motor.forward(50, 2, wait=True);
  • from your own main loop, every 10–50 ms.

The source is about 63 KB, much of it docstrings. Precompile it with mpy-cross and copy the .mpy to the board: .mpy files leave the docstrings out and skip on-board compilation, which can run out of RAM on an ESP32 without PSRAM.

Example 
from pingoblin_motor import MotorBoard

board = MotorBoard(a_en=25, a_ph=26, b_en=27, b_ph=33, sleep_pin=32, fault_pin=39)
board.enable_monitor(on_fault=print)
board.motor_a.forward(60, duration=2, wait=True)

docs.title: HalfBridgeMotor
docs.text:
HalfBridgeMotor(name, board, pin, driver, output, pins, pwm_freq=20000, **options)

Bases: Motor

One unidirectional motor in four-motor mode (JP1 all pads open).

Each DRV8874 output works on its own, so a board drives four motors: a1 (J4 A1, OUT1), a2 (J4 A2, OUT2), b1 (J5 B1) and b2 (J5 B2). Wire each motor between its output and a VM pin on J6. Create the motors through MotorBoard(mode="independent").

Input pin Output Motor Low Low-side on: OUT at 0 V Runs (full VM across it) High High-side on: OUT at VM Off, braking gently (nSLEEP low) Open Coasts

The motor runs while its input is low, so the library drives the pin at 1 − speed: forward(30) sets the pin to 70 % duty.

Differences from Motor:

  • One direction only: reverse() and negative speeds raise an error; no invert.
  • No current limit. The DRV8874 turns current regulation off in this mode.
  • No per-motor current: ISENSE is the sum of both motors on a driver. Read it with MotorBoard.driver_current().
  • coast() sleeps the drivers, so it works only when every other motor on the same nSLEEP line is idle. Otherwise the motor brakes.
Example 
board = MotorBoard(a_en=25, a_ph=26, b_en=27, b_ph=33, sleep_pin=32, fault_pin=39,
                   mode="independent")
board["a1"].forward(60)
board["b2"].forward(100, duration=3, wait=True)
board.close()          # stops all four and sleeps the drivers

The mode must match the PMODE jumper JP1:

mode JP1 Motors Names (default) "ph_en" Pads 1–2 (default) 2 × Motor a, b "pwm" Pads 2–3 2 × Motor a, b "independent" All pads open 4 × HalfBridgeMotor a1, a2, b1, b2

docs.title: HalfBridgeMotor
docs.text:
HalfBridgeMotor(name: str, board: 'MotorBoard', pin: int, *, driver: str, output: int, backend, pwm_frequency: float = 1000.0, **options)

Bases: Motor

One unidirectional brushed DC motor in four-motor mode (JP1 all pads open).

In this mode each DRV8874 output works on its own, so each board drives four motors: a1 (J4 A1, OUT1), a2 (J4 A2, OUT2), b1 (J5 B1) and b2 (J5 B2). Wire each motor between its output and one of the four VM pins on J6. Create the motors through MotorBoard with mode="independent", not directly.

How the output drives the motor:

Input pin Output Motor Low Low-side on: OUT at 0 V Runs (full VM across it) High High-side on: OUT at VM Off, braking gently (nSLEEP low) Open Coasts

The motor runs while its input is low, so the library drives the pin at 1 − speed: forward(30) sets the pin to 70 % duty. You don't need to invert anything yourself.

Differences from Motor:

  • One direction only. reverse() and negative speeds raise an error; invert is not allowed.
  • No current limit. The DRV8874 turns its current regulation off in this mode. A stalled motor draws its full stall current until the driver's overcurrent protection (about 6 A or more) or the board fuse trips.
  • No per-motor current reading. ISENSE carries the sum of both motors on one driver; read it with MotorBoard.driver_current(). Stall, open-load and overload checks per motor are not available.
  • coast() needs the drivers to sleep, so it coasts only when every other motor on the same nSLEEP line is idle. Otherwise the motor brakes.
Example 
from pingoblin_motor import MotorBoard

board = MotorBoard(a_en=12, a_ph=5, b_en=13, b_ph=6, sleep_pin=26, fault_pin=19,
                   mode="independent")
board["a1"].forward(60)                 # pump on at 60 %
board["b2"].forward(100, duration=3)    # fan on for 3 s
board["a1"].stop()
board.close()                           # stops all four and sleeps the drivers

docs.title: Current sensors
docs.text:
Current sensing: the ADS1115 driver and current-sensor classes.

Board A outputs 0.675 V per amp on A_ISENSE and B_ISENSE (J3 pins 7 and 8). One ADS1115 has four inputs, so it reads two boards (four motors). Up to four ADS1115 boards share one I²C bus (addresses 0x48 to 0x4B).

ISENSE is zero during the PWM off-time. The ADS1115 is a delta-sigma converter that averages each reading over about 1.2 ms, so with PWM at 1 kHz or faster one reading is roughly duty × motor current. Motor.read_current() divides by the duty to estimate the motor current.

docs.title: User Guide
docs.text:
Board A drives two brushed DC motors in both directions from any 3.3 V or 5 V microcontroller, such as a Raspberry Pi, ESP32, Raspberry Pi Pico or Arduino. Each motor has its own TI DRV8874 H-bridge, with speed set by PWM, direction set by one pin, and a current-sense output you can read with an ADC.

  • Two independent motor channels, motor supply 6–18 V (12 V nominal)
  • Direction + speed control (PH/EN, phase/enable mode), with a jumper for two-input PWM (pulse-width modulation) mode
  • Four-motor mode: up to four one-direction motors, such as pumps and fans
  • Analog current feedback per motor (0.675 V/A) for stall detection
  • Built-in current limit, overcurrent and over-temperature protection
  • Reverse-polarity protection, surge suppressor (TVS) and a 3 A resettable fuse on the motor supply
  • Push buttons to test each motor without writing code
  • Direction LEDs per motor, plus power and fault LEDs
  • Power through-terminal for daisy-chaining several boards from one supply
  • Safe start-up: motors stay off while the host boots (in four-motor mode this needs a 4.7 kΩ resistor on nSLEEP)

1. Find your way around the board: Board overview.

  3. Wire the board using Quick start.

docs.title: Test buttons and LEDs
docs.text:
Each motor has a FWD and a REV button that runs it at full speed while held. Use them to check the wiring before writing any code.

Button What it does SW1 A FWD Motor A forward (EN high, PH high: OUT1 positive) SW2 A REV Motor A reverse (EN high, PH low: OUT2 positive) SW3 B FWD Motor B forward SW4 B REV Motor B reverse
  • The buttons need VLOGIC (J3 pin 2). With no host connected, feed 3.3–5 V to VLOGIC from any source, such as a USB 5 V lead, and GND to J3 pin 1.
  • They are safe to press while a host is connected, even if the host is driving the pins low: 1 kΩ resistors protect the host's GPIOs.
  • They work as described here only in PH/EN mode (the default jumper setting). In PWM mode FWD brakes the motor and REV runs it forward. In four-motor mode the buttons can only turn motors off, and the direction LEDs don't show motor status: see buttons and LEDs in four-motor mode.

Pressing FWD and REV together gives forward

FWD drives both EN and PH high, while REV only drives EN, so FWD wins. The result is the same as pressing FWD alone and can't harm the board or the host. Release one button before pressing the other: flipping from forward to reverse at full speed causes a current surge (the fault LED flickers as the current limit catches it) and is hard on gearboxes.

docs.title: Configuration: PMODE jumper (JP1)
docs.text:
JP1 is a 3-pad solder jumper that sets the control mode for both drivers. It ships with pads 1–2 bridged (PH/EN mode).

  • PH/EN mode (phase/enable, default): one pin per motor sets the direction (PH) and the other turns the motor on and sets its speed (EN). One PWM channel per motor is enough.
  • PWM mode (IN1/IN2, input 1 / input 2): each pin drives one side of the motor directly. This matches two-input drivers such as the L298N and DRV8833, and lets each motor coast on its own, but needs PWM on both pins for full control.
  • Four-motor mode (all pads open): each pin drives one output on its own, so the board runs four one-direction motors, each wired between a motor terminal and the VM header J6. There is no current limit, and an undriven input turns its motor on, so it needs extra setup. See Four-motor mode.

See the Glossary for PWM, duty cycle and other terms.

Warning

Leaving all three pads open selects four-motor mode. Do this only on purpose: in that mode an input that isn't driven runs its motor at full speed. Read Four-motor mode first.

JP1 setting Mode J3 pin 3 / 5 J3 pin 4 / 6 Test buttons Library 1–2 bridged (default) PH/EN EN: on/off + PWM speed PH: direction Forward / reverse control mode="ph_en" 2–3 bridged PWM (IN1/IN2) IN1 IN2 Not supported: FWD brakes the motor and REV runs it forward mode="pwm" All open Four-motor Motor A1 / B1: low = on Motor A2 / B2: low = on Turn motors off only: see buttons in four-motor mode mode="independent"

To change it, cut the thin trace between pads 1 and 2 with a craft knife, check with a multimeter that they're open, then bridge pads 2 and 3 with solder (PWM mode) or leave all pads open (four-motor mode). The drivers read JP1 when they wake, so the new mode takes effect at the next power-up or wake from sleep.

Motor A; motor B is the same.

IN1 (pin 3) IN2 (pin 4) OUT1 OUT2 Motor Low Low Open Open Coast High Low High Low Forward Low High Low High Reverse High High Low Low Brake

PWM mode suits libraries written for two-input drivers such as the L298N or DRV8833 (gpiozero Motor, Arduino analogWrite on either pin). With gpiozero's Motor class, pass forward= J3 pin 3 (IN1) and backward= J3 pin 4 (IN2) so its directions match the table above.

In PWM mode each motor can coast on its own, without sleeping the board.

docs.title: Speed control in each mode
docs.text:
In every mode, speed comes from the PWM duty cycle: the fraction of each PWM period for which the motor is connected to the supply. A motor driven at 60% duty sees, on average, about 60% of VM, so it runs at roughly 60% of its full speed at that load. What differs between the modes is which pin you switch, and what the motor does in the off-time.

Mode Forward at speed d Reverse at speed d Off-time Response PH/EN (default) PH high, EN PWM at duty d PH low, EN PWM at duty d Brake Firm, close to linear PWM, slow decay (what the library uses) IN1 high, IN2 PWM at duty 1 − d IN2 high, IN1 PWM at duty 1 − d Brake The same as PH/EN PWM, fast decay IN1 PWM at duty d, IN2 low IN2 PWM at duty d, IN1 low Coast Softer; speed falls away at low duty Four-motor Input PWM at duty 1 − d (one direction only) Not available Brake (through the high side) The same as PH/EN

PH/EN mode. EN carries the speed and PH the direction, so a single PWM channel per motor is enough. During the off-time both low-side switches are on (brake, also called slow decay), so the motor's current keeps circulating and the speed follows the duty cycle closely, even at light load. This is the easiest mode to use and gives the best low-speed control. The library's speed_pc (0–100) is the EN duty cycle.

PWM mode, slow decay. One input is held high and the other is switched. The motor is driven while the switched input is low, so its duty is inverted: for 30% speed forward, hold IN1 high and run IN2 at 70%. The off-time is a brake, so the response matches PH/EN mode. The library does this inversion for you in mode="pwm".

PWM mode, fast decay. One input is held low and the other is switched at the speed duty, which is how most two-input motor libraries work, including gpiozero's Motor class and Arduino code that calls analogWrite() on one pin. In the off-time both outputs turn off and the motor coasts, while its current flows back into the supply. Expect less torque and a less linear response at low duty: a lightly loaded motor may barely slow until the duty is well below 50%. It works, but slow decay gives finer control.

docs.title: Practical limits
docs.text:
• Minimum speed. Most small motors don't start turning until the duty cycle reaches about 10–30%, because of friction and gearbox losses. Below that they hum without turning. The library's min_speed_pc raises any non-zero speed to this value.
  • PWM frequency. Use 20 kHz where the host supports it: it's above human hearing and gives smooth current. Lower frequencies (1–5 kHz, such as the Pi's software PWM) work the same way but make the motor whine.
  • Full speed. 100% duty applies the full supply to the motor. The test buttons drive EN high, so they always run at 100%.

100% duty and the current limit

The drivers limit current on every PWM cycle and restart on the next PWM edge. At exactly 100% duty there are no edges, so if a motor stalls and reaches the current limit, the driver holds it in brake (and lights the fault LED) until the input changes. To recover, change the speed, stop and restart, or release and press the test button again. If a stall is likely at full speed, run at 99% instead: the motor is effectively at full speed, and the current limit then recovers on its own.

docs.text:
The board has six connectors: two for power (see Powering the board), two for motors, one logic header (J3, see J3 pinout) and the VM header J6 for four-motor mode.

In parallel with J1 J4 MOTOR A 3.5 mm screw terminal OUT1 (A1) OUT2 (A2) Motor A J5 MOTOR B 3.5 mm screw terminal OUT1 (B1) OUT2 (B2) Motor B J6 VMx4 2.54 mm 2×2 header VM VM All four pins are VM. Motor polarity does not matter in PH/EN or PWM mode: if a motor turns the wrong way, swap its two wires or invert the direction in code (the library's invert option). In four-motor mode each motor runs one way only, so connect its + lead to J6 and its − lead to the terminal. Screw terminals take wire up to about 18 AWG. You can also solder wires straight into the pads.

J6 is the motor supply

J6 carries VM, the full motor supply (up to 18 V). Use it only for motors in four-motor mode. Never connect it to J3 or to the host.

The connectors are supplied loose, so you can fit screw terminals, headers or solder wires directly.

Reduce motor noise

Brushed motors spark at their brushes and are the main source of electrical noise in a motor project. Solder a 100 nF ceramic capacitor directly across the motor's own terminals (at the motor, not at the board), and twist the two motor wires together along their length. This keeps the noise out of your host's ADC readings, wireless signals and nearby electronics.

docs.title: Controlling the motors
docs.text:
Terms used on this page

  • PWM (pulse-width modulation): the host switches a pin on and off rapidly, many thousands of times a second. The duty cycle is the percentage of each cycle the pin is on, and it sets the average power, and so the speed, of the motor.
  • PH (phase): the direction input. High runs the motor forward, low runs it in reverse.
  • EN (enable): the drive input. High drives the motor, low brakes it. Feeding it PWM sets the speed.
  • IN1 / IN2 (input 1 / input 2): in PWM mode, the same two pins become two direct inputs, each controlling one side of the motor (OUT1 and OUT2).
  • nSLEEP / nFAULT: the leading n means the signal is active when low: nSLEEP low puts the drivers to sleep, and nFAULT goes low on a fault or current limiting.

The Glossary lists every abbreviation used in this manual.

This page covers the two-motor modes. For up to four one-direction motors, see Four-motor mode.

In the default PH/EN (phase/enable) mode, each motor needs two pins: EN (enable) turns it on and sets the speed with PWM (pulse-width modulation), and PH (phase) sets the direction. This is the same scheme as gpiozero's PhaseEnableMotor, except that gpiozero calls PH low "forward" (see below). The table is for motor A; motor B is identical using B_EN and B_PH.

nSLEEP A_EN A_PH OUT1 OUT2 Motor LED High (default) Low Any Low Low Brake (stops quickly) Off High High / PWM High High Low Forward Green High High / PWM Low Low High Reverse Red Low Any Any Open Open Coast (sleep, near-zero current) Off

Speed: drive EN with PWM. The duty cycle sets the speed, and in the PWM off-time the motor brakes, which gives a firm, linear response. Use 20 kHz to keep the motor quiet. 1–5 kHz also works but makes the motor whine. See Speed control in each mode for how duty cycle maps to speed in each mode, and the limits at very low and 100% duty.

Changing direction: change PH at any time. To protect gearboxes, slow down or stop briefly before reversing a heavily loaded motor. The library does this for you: it brakes for reverse_delay (0.1 s by default) before reversing a running motor.

Sleep / emergency stop: pull nSLEEP low to put both drivers to sleep (outputs open, motors coast). Wake-up takes about 1 ms. nSLEEP is pulled high on the board, so the drivers are awake whenever VLOGIC is present.

Start-up behaviour: EN and PH have pull-down resistors, so while the host is booting (pins floating) both motors are held in brake.

"Forward" and "reverse" here follow TI's convention for the DRV8874: PH high = forward, with OUT1 positive (green LED). Which way the shaft actually turns depends on how the motor is wired; swap its two leads, or use invert=True in the library, to change it.

Coast and nSLEEP

In PH/EN mode the only way to coast is to sleep the driver, and nSLEEP is shared by both motors. The library's coast() therefore sleeps the board only when the other motor is idle, and otherwise brakes. In PWM mode each motor coasts on its own.

docs.title: Driving the pins directly
docs.text:
The library is the easiest way to use the board, but the protocol is simple enough to drive by hand. Speed runs from −1.0 (full reverse) to 1.0 (full forward).

ESP32, MicroPythonRaspberry Pi, gpiozero 
from machine import Pin, PWM, ADC
import time

A_EN = PWM(Pin(25), freq=20000, duty_u16=0)   # J3 pin 3
A_PH = Pin(26, Pin.OUT, value=0)              # J3 pin 4
A_SENSE = ADC(Pin(34)); A_SENSE.atten(ADC.ATTN_11DB)  # J3 pin 7
FAULT = Pin(39, Pin.IN)                       # J3 pin 10 (pulled up on board)

def drive(en, ph, speed):
    """speed -1.0..1.0; positive = forward (PH high, OUT1 positive)."""
    ph.value(1 if speed > 0 else 0)
    en.duty_u16(int(min(abs(speed), 1.0) * 65535))

def amps(adc):
    return adc.read_uv() / 1_000_000 / 0.675   # 0.675 V per amp

drive(A_EN, A_PH, 0.6)
for _ in range(30):
    a = amps(A_SENSE)
    print("Motor A: %.2f A  fault/limit: %s" % (a, FAULT.value() == 0))
    if a > 1.6:              # about 80% of the 2 A limit at 3.3 V logic
        print("Stall - stopping")
        break
    time.sleep(0.1)
drive(A_EN, A_PH, 0)         # EN low = brake

from gpiozero import PhaseEnableMotor, DigitalInputDevice
from time import sleep

motor_a = PhaseEnableMotor(phase=5, enable=12)   # J3 pins 4, 3
motor_b = PhaseEnableMotor(phase=6, enable=13)   # J3 pins 6, 5
motor_a.enable_device.frequency = 1000           # software PWM
motor_b.enable_device.frequency = 1000
fault = DigitalInputDevice(19, pull_up=None, active_state=False)  # J3 pin 10

# gpiozero's forward() drives PH low, which is this board's reverse,
# so backward() runs a motor forward here.
motor_a.backward(0.5)   # forward (OUT1 positive, green LED)
motor_b.forward(0.75)   # reverse (OUT2 positive, red LED)
sleep(2)
print("Fault or current limit:", fault.is_active)
motor_a.stop()   # brake
motor_b.stop()

gpiozero uses software PWM, which is unreliable above about 1 kHz, so the motors may whine. For silent 20 kHz drive on a Pi, use the hardware PWM pins (GPIO12, GPIO13).

docs.title: Current sensing and current limit
docs.text:
A_ISENSE and B_ISENSE output 0.675 V for every amp flowing in that motor. Read them with an ADC to measure load or detect a stall. On a Raspberry Pi, use a PinGoblin ADS1115 board; an ESP32 or Pico can use its own ADC.

\[ I_{motor} = \frac{V_{ISENSE}}{0.675\ \mathrm{V/A}} \]
  • The reading is only valid while the motor is driven (EN high). During PWM off-time it drops to zero, so average several samples, or sample in the PWM on-time. The library does this for you (see Current sensing in the API).
  • A stalled motor shows as a reading that sits at the current limit while the shaft isn't turning. A typical approach: if the reading stays above about 80% of the limit for more than 200 ms, stop the motor. The library's stall detection works this way.
  • Each driver limits motor current on every PWM cycle (cycle-by-cycle chopping). The limit is set from VLOGIC:
Host logic (VLOGIC) Current limit per motor ISENSE at the limit 3.3 V About 2.0 A About 1.32 V 5.0 V About 3.0 A About 2.0 V
  • While limiting, the red fault LED lights and nFAULT goes low. Normal operation resumes on the next PWM cycle once the load drops. At exactly 100% duty there is no next cycle, so the motor stays braked until the input changes: see 100% duty and the current limit.
  • A short circuit or overheating shuts the driver down. It retries automatically once the fault clears.
  • In four-motor mode there is no current limit, and each ISENSE output carries the combined current of the two motors on that driver.
  • Both motors share the 3 A board fuse. If both run near their limit at 5 V logic for more than a few seconds, the fuse will trip. Once power is removed it resets within about a minute.

docs.title: Is ISENSE related to motor speed?
docs.text:
Not directly. ISENSE measures current, and in a brushed DC motor current follows the load torque, not the speed. At a fixed supply voltage and PWM duty, current and speed are linearly related but in opposite directions: as load slows the motor, its back-EMF falls and the current rises.

\[ \omega = \frac{D \cdot V_{M} - I \cdot R}{K_e} \]

Here \(\omega\) is motor speed, \(D\) the PWM duty (0–1), \(V_M\) the motor supply voltage, \(I\) the motor current (\(V_{ISENSE} / 0.675\)), \(R\) the motor's winding resistance and \(K_e\) its back-EMF constant.

What this means in practice:

  • Fixed duty and supply: speed and current fall on a straight line. Speed is highest at the no-load current and zero at the stall current.
  • Change the duty or the supply: the line shifts, so the same current can mean very different speeds. ISENSE alone can't tell you RPM.
  • No load: a free-running motor draws almost the same small current at any speed, because only friction loads it. ISENSE barely changes with RPM.

For a rough speed estimate at one fixed duty, calibrate two points. Measure the no-load speed \(\omega_0\) and current \(I_0\), then the stall current \(I_{stall}\) (hold the shaft for under a second). Then:

\[ \omega \approx \omega_0 \cdot \frac{I_{stall} - I}{I_{stall} - I_0} \]

Limits of this estimate:

  • The current limit (2 A or 3 A) clamps the current, so the line ends there. Any load heavier than that just reads as the limit.
  • Winding resistance rises about 0.4% per °C as the motor warms, which shifts the line.
  • Gearbox friction and brush noise add error. Average several readings.

For real speed measurement or closed-loop speed control, use a motor with an encoder (many hobby gearmotors have a Hall encoder) and read it on the host. Use ISENSE for load and stall detection.

docs.title: Daisy-chaining boards
docs.text: Several boards can share one motor supply and one host.

docs.title: Power
docs.text:
• Connect one power source to the first board (J1 or J2), then wire J2 of each board to J2 of the next. Only one power source for the whole chain: see Powering the board.
  • J1 and J2 are wired in parallel, so every board's terminals carry the current of all the boards after it. Keep the total current through any board's terminals at or below 6 A. For more boards, run a separate supply lead (a star) to each group.
  • Each board still has its own 3 A fuse.

docs.title: Logic
docs.text:
• Each board needs its own EN and PH pins (J3 pins 3–6).
  • nSLEEP (pin 9) and nFAULT (pin 10) can be shared: wire them together across boards and connect them to one GPIO each. That gives one emergency-stop line and one fault line. nFAULT is open-drain, so any board can pull the shared line low.
  • Connect GND (pin 1) and VLOGIC (pin 2) on every board.
  • One PinGoblin ADS1115 board reads the ISENSE outputs of two boards. Up to four ADS1115 boards share one I2C bus.

In software, manage the boards as one MotorChain.

docs.title: Four-motor mode
docs.text:
In four-motor mode, each DRV8874 runs its two outputs separately instead of as one H-bridge. Each output can then drive its own one-direction (unidirectional) motor, so one board drives up to four. This suits pumps, fans, blowers and other motors that only ever turn one way. Each motor connects between one of the motor terminals and one of the four VM pins on J6.

PH/EN or PWM mode Four-motor mode Motors per board 2, both directions 4, one direction each Motor wiring Across J4 or J5 From one J4 / J5 terminal to a J6 VM pin Current limit 2 A (3.3 V logic) or 3 A (5 V logic) per motor None Current sensing Per motor Per pair: A1 + A2, B1 + B2 Coast one motor on its own PWM mode only No (only by sleeping the whole board) JP1 Pads 1–2 or 2–3 bridged All three pads open

An input that isn't driven turns its motor on

In four-motor mode a motor runs while its input is low. The board's pull-down resistors, which keep the motors stopped in the other modes, hold every input low. So whenever the drivers are awake and the host isn't actively driving the inputs high (while the host boots, after your program exits or crashes, or with J3 unplugged but VLOGIC present), all four motors run at full speed with no current limit.

Before using this mode:

  1. Wire nSLEEP (J3 pin 9) to a GPIO on the host.
  2. Fit a 4.7 kΩ resistor from J3 pin 9 to J3 pin 1 (GND). If several boards share one nSLEEP line, use a single 2.2 kΩ resistor on that line instead (up to four boards).

The resistor overrides the board's 100 kΩ pull-up on nSLEEP, so the drivers sleep (outputs open, motors off) unless your program holds nSLEEP high. The library keeps the drivers asleep until the first run command, and puts them to sleep again when the board is closed. Check it: with your program stopped and VLOGIC present, nSLEEP should measure below 0.5 V and no motor should turn.

docs.title: Setting up
docs.text:
1. Set JP1 to all pads open. Cut the thin trace between pads 1 and 2 with a craft knife. Leave pads 2 and 3 unbridged. Check with a multimeter that pad 2 is open to both pad 1 and pad 3. The drivers read JP1 each time they wake, so the change takes effect at the next wake-up or power-up.
  2. Fit the nSLEEP resistor and wire nSLEEP to a GPIO, as described above.
  3. Wire the motors. Connect each motor between its terminal and any of the four pins on J6. J6 carries VM: the motor supply after the fuse and reverse-polarity protection.
  4. Check the direction. Current flows from VM, through the motor, into the terminal. Connect the motor's + lead to J6 and its − lead to the terminal, so it turns the way it would on a battery. To reverse it, swap its two leads.
Motor Terminal Controlled by Library name A1 J4 A1 (OUT1 of U1) J3 pin 3 (A_EN) a1 A2 J4 A2 (OUT2 of U1) J3 pin 4 (A_PH) a2 B1 J5 B1 (OUT1 of U2) J3 pin 5 (B_EN) b1 B2 J5 B2 (OUT2 of U2) J3 pin 6 (B_PH) b2

The terminal labels A1, A2, B1 and B2 are printed on the board next to J4 and J5.

You don't need all four motors: leave unused terminals empty. You also don't need external flyback diodes. When an input goes high, the driver's high-side switch carries the motor's current back to VM. That makes this mode suitable for solenoids and valves too.

Reduce motor noise

As in the other modes, solder a 100 nF ceramic capacitor across each motor's own terminals and twist its two wires together.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Each output is a half-bridge: one switch to VM and one to ground. The input selects which switch is on.

nSLEEP Input Output Motor High Low Low-side on: 0 V Runs: full VM across it High High High-side on: VM Off. Both motor leads are at VM, so it brakes gently Low Any Open Off, coasting (drivers asleep)

docs.title: Speed
docs.text: Speed comes from the PWM duty cycle, as in the other modes, but the motor is driven while the input is low. The duty is therefore inverted: for 30% speed, the input is low 30% of the time, so it runs at 70% duty. The library does this inversion for you. During the off-time the motor brakes through the high-side switch, so the speed follows the duty cycle closely, like slow decay in the other modes. See Speed control in each mode for the practical limits on minimum speed and PWM frequency.

docs.title: No current limit
docs.text:
The DRV8874 turns its current regulation off in this mode, so the current limit set by VLOGIC doesn't apply. A stalled motor draws its full stall current. What still protects the board:

  • each driver's overcurrent shutdown, which trips at several amps and retries automatically;
  • the drivers' over-temperature shutdown;
  • the 3 A resettable fuse, shared by all four motors.

Choose motors whose running current, all four together, stays under 3 A. Keep each pair (A1 + A2, or B1 + B2) under about 2 A continuous, which is the same thermal budget as one motor in the other modes. If the board fuse keeps tripping, a motor is probably stalling or the total load is too high.

docs.title: Current sensing
docs.text:
ISENSE now measures the low-side current of both outputs of a driver together. A_ISENSE reads A1 + A2, and B_ISENSE reads B1 + B2, at the usual 0.675 V per amp. Averaged over several samples, it gives the supply current the pair draws. The library reads it with board.driver_current("a"). Per-motor stall detection isn't possible in this mode, because the board can't tell the two motors apart.

nFAULT, and the red fault LED, now only signal a real driver fault: an overcurrent, over-temperature or undervoltage shutdown.

docs.title: Test buttons and LEDs in four-motor mode
docs.text:
The test buttons can only turn motors off in this mode, never on. Pressing a button pulls its inputs high, and a high input is "off". When no program is driving nSLEEP high, the drivers are asleep and the buttons do nothing.

Button While held SW1 A FWD A1 and A2 off (drives both A_EN and A_PH high) SW2 A REV A1 off (drives A_EN high) SW3 B FWD B1 and B2 off SW4 B REV B1 off

A button press overrides your program, so a motor can stop while the software still reports it running.

The direction LEDs sit across each driver's two outputs, so they light only when the two outputs differ. They show the difference between a pair of motors, not what either motor is doing. For driver A (D8 green, D9 red; D13 and D14 work the same way for driver B):

A1 A2 J4 A1 / A2 LEDs Off Off VM / VM Both off Running Off 0 V / VM Red Off Running VM / 0 V Green Running Running 0 V / 0 V Both off Asleep Asleep Open Both off

With PWM speed control, the LEDs glow dimly and may flicker, depending on how the two duty cycles overlap. Ignore the direction LEDs in this mode.

The other LEDs work normally. The green power LED shows the motor supply, and the red fault LED shows a driver shutdown.

docs.title: Using the library
docs.text:
Pass mode="independent" and a sleep_pin. The board then has four motors named a1, a2, b1 and b2 (or your own names). Each one has the usual forward(), run(), stop(), speed_pc, duration= and ramp options, but no reverse().

from pingoblin_motor import MotorBoard

with MotorBoard(a_en=12, a_ph=5, b_en=13, b_ph=6, sleep_pin=26, fault_pin=19,
                mode="independent") as board:
    board["a1"].forward(60)                    # J4 A1 at 60 %
    board["b2"].forward(100, duration=3, wait=True)
    print(board.driver_current("a"))           # A1 + A2, if a sensor is configured

The MicroPython library works the same way. See HalfBridgeMotor in the API reference.

docs.title: Driving the pins directly
docs.text: Without the library, set the inputs high before you drive nSLEEP high, and drive nSLEEP low before your program releases the pins. To run a motor at speed s (0–1), drive its input with PWM at duty 1 − s. A steady high stops it; a steady low runs it at full speed.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Abbreviations and terms used in this manual, in alphabetical order.

docs.title: J3 pinout
docs.text:
J3 is a single row of 10 pins on the left edge of the board. Looking at the component side, pin 10 (nFAULT) is at the top and pin 1 (GND, square pad) is at the bottom, nearest the test buttons.

Pin Signal Direction PH/EN mode (default) PWM mode Four-motor mode 10 nFAULT Output Low = fault or current limiting Same Low = driver fault 9 nSLEEP Input Low = sleep, both motors coast Same Must be driven high to run. Needs a GPIO and a 4.7 kΩ pull-down 8 B_ISENSE Output Motor B current, 0.675 V/A Same Motors B1 + B2 together 7 A_ISENSE Output Motor A current, 0.675 V/A Same Motors A1 + A2 together 6 B_PH Input Motor B direction IN2, motor B Motor B2, low = on 5 B_EN Input Motor B on / speed (PWM) IN1, motor B Motor B1, low = on 4 A_PH Input Motor A direction IN2, motor A Motor A2, low = on 3 A_EN Input Motor A on / speed (PWM) IN1, motor A Motor A1, low = on 2 VLOGIC Power Logic supply in, 3.3–5 V Same Same 1 GND Power Ground, common with the host Same Same

All signal pins work at 3.3 V or 5 V logic, matching whatever you feed to VLOGIC. Inputs have pull-downs (pull-up on nSLEEP), so unused inputs can be left open in PH/EN and PWM modes. In four-motor mode an open input turns its motor on: see Four-motor mode. nFAULT is open-drain with a 10 kΩ pull-up to VLOGIC. The ISENSE outputs never exceed VLOGIC.

Signal names: EN = enable (on/off and PWM speed), PH = phase (direction), IN1 / IN2 = input 1 / input 2 (PWM mode), ISENSE = current sense output. A leading n (nSLEEP, nFAULT) means the signal is active when low.

The mode is set by the PMODE jumper.

docs.title: Powering the board
docs.text:
The board runs from 6–18 V DC. It has two power connectors, wired in parallel:

Connector Type Use J1 XT30, right-angle male Batteries and supplies with an XT30 plug J2 5.08 mm screw terminal (pin 1 VIN+, pin 2 GND) Wired supplies, or power out to the next board

The board draws up to 3 A in total (both motors). The supply or battery must be able to deliver that, plus the motors' start-up surge.

One power source per chain

J1 and J2 are connected together, and so is every board in a daisy chain. Never connect a battery and a supply at the same time, on this board or any other board in the chain: the supply would push current into the battery with no charge control.

docs.title: One pack (6.0–8.4 V)
docs.text: Plug a PinGoblin QUAD or DUAL pack (from the UPS HAT+) straight into J1. The board runs normally, but motors rated for 12 V run at roughly two-thirds of their 12 V speed.

docs.title: Two packs in series (12.0–16.8 V)
docs.text:
Two packs in series give 14.4 V nominal: the right supply for 12 V motors, solenoids and steppers. Join them with an XT30 series lead:

Lead connector Type Connects to Input A XT30 male (cable) Pack A Input B XT30 male (cable) Pack B Output XT30 female (cable) J1 on the board

Inside the lead, using 18 AWG wire:

  • Input A − to Output −
  • Input A + to Input B −
  • Input B + to Output +

Rules for two packs:

  • Use two packs of the same type (both QUAD or both DUAL), fully charged on the UPS HAT+ before use, and switch both on.
  • Charge each pack on its own on the UPS HAT+. Never charge through the series lead.
  • If either pack's protection switches off, the whole string stops. That's safe: recharge both packs.

Never plug the series lead into a UPS HAT+

The lead outputs up to 16.8 V. The UPS HAT+ battery input is for one 2S pack (8.4 V maximum) and will be destroyed. Label the lead "MOTOR BOARDS ONLY – 16.8 V".

docs.title: Low battery
docs.text:
The board has no low-voltage cut-off: it keeps running until the packs' own protection switches off at 2.8 V per cell (5.6 V for one pack, 11.2 V for two). That's safe, but regularly discharging that far shortens cell life. For the longest life, stop at 3.1 V per cell, where the UPS HAT+ software stops:

Packs Full Stop at Packs switch off at One 8.4 V 6.2 V 5.6 V Two in series 16.8 V 12.4 V 11.2 V

To measure the supply from your host, use a resistor divider into an ADC input (for example 100 kΩ over 22 kΩ, which gives 3.0 V at 16.8 V).

docs.title: Other batteries
docs.text:
Any battery with its own protection circuit (BMS), an XT30 plug and a full-charge voltage of 18 V or less:

Battery Full charge Suitable? 2S Li-ion / LiPo 8.4 V Yes 3S Li-ion / LiPo 12.6 V Yes 4S Li-ion / LiPo 16.8 V Yes 4S LiFePO4 14.6 V Yes 12 V lead-acid / AGM 13.8–14.7 V while charging Yes 5S Li-ion / LiPo or more 21 V or more No

docs.title: Wired supplies
docs.text: Connect plug-packs and bench supplies to J2: positive to pin 1 (VIN+), negative to pin 2 (GND). Keep the supply at or below 18 V, including its tolerance: a supply labelled 18 V can measure higher. A 12 V supply suits most hobby motors.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
Wire J3 to the host first, then the motors, then the motor supply last.

  1. With everything unpowered, connect J3 to the host using the table below. You need at least GND, VLOGIC, and one EN and one PH pin per motor.
  2. Connect each motor to J4 (A) or J5 (B). For less electrical noise, solder a 100 nF capacitor across each motor's terminals and twist its leads (see Connectors).
  3. Connect power: a battery to J1 (XT30), or a 6–18 V supply to J2 (positive to VIN+, negative to GND). See Powering the board. The green power LED lights.
  4. Power the host. Motors stay stopped (braked) until the host drives an EN pin high.
  5. Optional: press a FWD or REV test button to check each motor turns before writing any code.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:

On an ESP32, avoid the boot-strapping pins (GPIO0, 2, 12, 15) and GPIO14, which toggles during boot. Use ADC1 pins for current sense, because ADC2 cannot be read while Wi-Fi is on. Leave nSLEEP unconnected if you don't need it: the board pulls it high.

docs.title: First program
docs.text:
Install the library (see Installation), then:

Raspberry PiMicroPython (ESP32)MicroPython (Pico) 
from pingoblin_motor import MotorBoard

board = MotorBoard(a_en=12, a_ph=5, b_en=13, b_ph=6, sleep_pin=26, fault_pin=19)
board.start_monitor(on_fault=print)        # stall and fault detection

board.motor_a.forward(60, duration=2, wait=True)   # 60 % for 2 s, then brake
board.motor_b.reverse(40)
board.motor_b.speed_pc = 80                # change speed while running
board.motor_b.coast()                      # spin down freely
board.close()

from pingoblin_motor import MotorBoard

board = MotorBoard(a_en=25, a_ph=26, b_en=27, b_ph=33, sleep_pin=32, fault_pin=39)
board.enable_monitor(on_fault=print)

board.motor_a.forward(60, duration=2, wait=True)   # blocks, still checks faults
board.motor_b.reverse(40)
board.pause(1.5)                                   # sleep that keeps checking faults
board.coast_all()

from pingoblin_motor import MotorBoard

board = MotorBoard(a_en=2, a_ph=3, b_en=4, b_ph=5, sleep_pin=6, fault_pin=7)
board.enable_monitor(on_fault=print)
board.motor_a.forward(60, duration=2, wait=True)

On a Raspberry Pi the library uses 1 kHz software PWM by default, which makes motors whine. For silent 20 kHz drive, use hardware PWM on GPIO12 and GPIO13: see PWM frequency. MicroPython boards use 20 kHz hardware PWM by default.

docs.title: Important safety information
docs.text:
Read these before connecting power.

Never connect VIN (6–18 V) to J3

J3 is logic only. VIN on any J3 pin will destroy the host and the drivers.

  • Do not exceed 18 V on VIN, including supply tolerance. A supply labelled 18 V can measure higher: check it with a meter, or use a lower voltage. The surge suppressor starts conducting at about 20 V and is not meant to carry continuous current.
  • Connect GND between the board and the host. J3 pin 1 must go to a host GND pin.
  • Wire with the power off. Connect and disconnect motors only while the supply is off.
  • The drivers get hot. At high currents the chips and the board around them can exceed 60 °C. Allow airflow and do not touch them while running.
  • Daisy-chaining: the VIN through-terminal (J2) shares one supply between boards. Keep the total current through a board's terminals at or below 6 A.
  • One power source per chain. J1 and J2 are connected together. Never connect a battery and a supply at the same time: see Powering the board.
  • Four-motor mode has no current limit, and an input that isn't driven turns its motor on. Fit the nSLEEP pull-down described in Four-motor mode before connecting motors.
  • Use a fused or current-limited supply. The on-board fuse protects the board, not your wiring or batteries.

docs.title: Specifications
docs.text:
Parameter Value Motor supply (VIN) 6–18 V DC (18 V maximum, including supply tolerance), 12 V nominal Logic supply (VLOGIC) 3.3–5 V, from the host Logic input high 1.5 V min (3.3 V and 5 V logic both work) Motor channels 2, bidirectional, or 4, one direction each (four-motor mode) Continuous current per motor About 1.5–2 A at 25 °C (to be confirmed by prototype thermal tests) Total board current 3 A continuous (resettable fuse: 3 A hold, 6 A trip) Current limit per motor About 2.0 A with 3.3 V logic, about 3.0 A with 5 V logic (none in four-motor mode) Current-sense output 0.675 V per amp PWM frequency Up to 100 kHz (20 kHz recommended, which is above human hearing) Driver IC TI DRV8874 (×2) Connectors XT30 right-angle male and 5.08 mm screw terminal (power), 3.5 mm screw terminals (motors), 2.54 mm 10-pin header (logic), 2.54 mm 2×2 header (VM, four-motor mode) Mounting M2.5 holes

20 kHz and pets

20 kHz is above human hearing, but dogs, cats and some other animals can hear it. The motor windings make only a faint sound at this frequency; if an animal seems bothered, raise the PWM frequency (the DRV8874 accepts up to 100 kHz).
